idiom_name: GameObject holding a List<Component>; ECS frameworks (Artemis, Ashley) for storage
implementation_notes: Plain Java writes the roles by hand, exactly as the Java Design Patterns catalogue shows: a Component interface (or abstract class) with one lifecycle method, a GameObject that owns either named component fields or a List<Component>, and static factory methods (createPlayer/createNpc) that assemble each entity kind - composition is the documented answer to Java's single inheritance, so nothing in the JDK supplies the container. When entity counts and component combinations grow, an ECS framework takes over storage and dispatch: Artemis-odb and libGDX Ashley keep components as plain POJOs in per-type bags and run systems over entities matched by their component set, so the entity object disappears and become id-based.
pitfalls: A List<Component> erases the component's type, so retrieving a capability means instanceof/stream filters and a missing component fails at runtime, not at compile time.
Nothing stops two components of the same class from being added; enforce one instance per type in add() or the entity updates the same capability twice.
Java interfaces with default methods invite shared mutable state as static fields or singletons on the interface - that state is process-wide and shared by every entity.

variants.name: ECS framework (Artemis-odb / libGDX Ashley) with component bags and systems
variants.idiom_name: Artemis-odb World/EntitySystem or Ashley Engine/EntitySystem with POJO components
variants.implementation_notes: The framework owns the entity ids and stores components per type, so behaviour is written as systems iterating entities that match a component family; the entity class itself is replaced by an id and the 'pluggable parts' become data-only POJOs. Choose it for large or data-driven entity populations; keep the hand-written bag for a handful of entity kinds, where the framework's wiring and systems are more code than the container it replaces.
pitfalls: Systems see components, not objects: whole-entity invariants have to be enforced by a dedicated system or the framework's aspect filters, not by a method on the entity.
Component classes must be POJOs with a no-arg constructor (frameworks pool and copy them); logic or references in a component break packing and copying.
System execution order is framework configuration, so a wrong order produces silent behaviour changes with no compile-time signal.
